title: The Lower East Side

cards: Five flights of narrow stairs. At the top, a small apartment: a kitchen, a front room, and a dark room in between with no window at all.
In the front room a sewing machine is already running before sunrise, because the family is paid by the piece. A boarder sleeps on two chairs pushed together.
Down in the street, pushcarts sell herring, pickles, pots and eyeglasses. And a few blocks away, tonight, a theater will fill with people laughing and weeping in Yiddish. Today, the Lower East Side.

teach.b: The Lower East Side is a neighborhood in Manhattan, and for the Jewish families of the great wave it was often the first address in America, shared with Italian, Irish and other immigrant neighbors.
Start with the tenements: apartment buildings packed tight, room after room, with little light or air. Toilets were in the hall or the yard. Families took in boarders to make the rent.
Over time, reformers pushed for laws that required windows, light and better plumbing, because the buildings themselves were making people sick. Then the work.
A great deal of it was in the garment trade: cutting, sewing, pressing, in small crowded shops called sweatshops, or at the kitchen table, paid by the piece.
Long days, low pay, and the boss could always find someone newer and hungrier. And yet the same streets were full of life.
Yiddish newspapers, with letters from readers asking for advice about love, work and faith. Synagogues in storefronts and in grand buildings. Cafés full of arguments.
And the Yiddish theater, where tired workers paid a little to watch family dramas, comedies, even Shakespeare in Yiddish, and wept openly in their seats.
A psalm holds up the picture these families were working toward: "When thou eatest the labour of thy hands, happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee." Not riches.
Just eating from your own work, and having it be enough.
In the tenements, the labor was brutal and the bread was thin. But people kept singing, praying and going to the theater, and their children climbed down those five flights to school.

how: Jewish families, museums and synagogues on the Lower East Side keep the tenement stories, and Psalm 128 is sung or read in Jewish life, including in some communities at weddings.

games.q: you've worked six long days sewing by the piece in a tenement. you have a few coins left over. what do you do with them?
o: buy a ticket to the Yiddish theater.
games.why: tired workers paid a little to watch dramas, comedies and even Shakespeare in Yiddish. the streets were hard, and full of life.

practice: Look at one thing near you, your shirt, your chair, your food, and follow it back: someone sewed it, built it, picked it, packed it.
Let one of those unseen workers become real in your mind, tired hands and a long shift, and hold them for a few breaths with respect.

wordCard.voice: Pushcarts. The carts that filled the streets of the Lower East Side, selling herring, pickles, pots and eyeglasses right outside the tenements. Today's word.
